# **Production Routing and Time-Study Analysis for High-End Outdoor Aluminum Furniture Manufacturing**

## **Introduction to Lean Production Systems in Premium Furniture Fabrication**

The manufacturing of high-end, heavy-duty outdoor furniture requires a delicate and precise synchronization between heavy industrial fabrication processes, such as metal cutting, welding, and sintered stone computer numerical control (CNC) routing, and the meticulous craftsmanship inherent in upholstery and powder coating. To establish a highly efficient, scalable, and balanced production line for premium brands, industrial engineering principles must be rigorously applied to calculate Standard Allowed Minutes (SAM), establish accurate cycle times, and determine the optimal Takt time for continuous flow1. Takt time, derived from the German word for rhythm or heartbeat, dictates the maximum allowable time to produce one unit to meet customer demand, acting as the foundational metric for line balancing2.

In a modern production facility utilizing 6061 and 6063 aluminum extrusions, performance acrylic fabrics, high-density reticulated foam, and ultra-compact sintered stone slabs, the variability of material processing demands a robust work measurement system. The primary objective of this comprehensive engineering report is to define the standard times for typical work centers required to produce a flagship product line. The analysis is specifically modeled around the fabrication of a standard 34-inch by 34-inch outdoor club chair frame, accompanied by a standard 24-inch by 24-inch box cushion and a 72-inch by 36-inch sintered stone dining tabletop. The formulation of these time standards utilizes predetermined motion time systems, primarily the Maynard Operation Sequence Technique (MOST), alongside continuous time studies, kinematic analyses, and strict adherence to the International Labour Organization (ILO) standards for Personal, Fatigue, and Delay (PF\&D) allowances2.

## **Work Measurement Methodologies and Allowance Formulation**

To engineer accurate and reliable routing databases for an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system, a clear distinction must be made between "Normal Time" and "Standard Time." Normal Time represents the exact duration an experienced, fully trained operator takes to perform a specific task at a 100 percent performance rating, without any interruptions6. Standard Time represents the realistic time required to complete a task under normal operating conditions on the factory floor, which must be inclusive of necessary physiological breaks, mental fatigue, and unavoidable operational delays6.

### **The Maynard Operation Sequence Technique**

The Maynard Operation Sequence Technique (MOST) is utilized to break manual operations down into fundamental sequence models, such as General Move, Controlled Move, and Tool Use5. Because the MOST methodology relies on predetermined motion times rather than subjective stopwatch estimations on the floor, it effectively eliminates performance rating biases and provides a highly accurate, universally accepted baseline for manual assembly, machine loading, and material handling tasks8. This calculated baseline forms the unadjusted Normal Time before physiological and environmental allowance multipliers are applied to the labor routing.

### **ILO Allowances and PF\&D Calculations**

No human operator can sustain a 100 percent performance pace indefinitely. Setting labor standards without adequate allowances leads to severe worker fatigue, diminished product quality, and high turnover6. The International Labour Organization (ILO) mandates the application of fatigue and personal allowances to ensure humane, sustainable, and realistic production standards4. The traditional and legally defensible standard for Personal, Fatigue, and Delay (PF\&D) in general manufacturing is an aggregate 15 percent allowance10.

A granular breakdown of the ILO allowance tables reveals how this allowance is typically distributed across different work centers based on the specific environmental and physiological demands of the task. The allowances are generally split into constant and variable categories.

&nbsp;

| Allowance Category | Component Description | Standard Percentage Allowance | Environmental/Task Triggers |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Constant Allowance** | Personal Needs | 5.0% | Restroom breaks, hydration, general well-being4. |
| **Constant Allowance** | Basic Fatigue | 4.0% | Energy expenditure for light work and basic monotony4. |
| **Variable Allowance** | Posture | 2.0% to 7.0% | Standing (2%), awkward bending (2%), lying/stretching (7%)12. |
| **Variable Allowance** | Visual Attention | 2.0% to 5.0% | Fine or exacting work (2%), very exacting work (5%)12. |
| **Variable Allowance** | Acoustic/Thermal | 1.0% to 5.0% | Intermittent loud noise (2%), high heat/humidity (1-5%)4. |
| **Unavoidable Delay** | Operational Interruption | 1.5% to 5.0% | Machine setup, material shortages, quality checks6. |

For the routing database outlined in this analysis, a baseline 15 percent PF\&D allowance multiplier (1.15) is applied to general assembly, automated cutting, sewing, and powder coating operations10. However, a specialized 20 percent PF\&D allowance multiplier (1.20) is strictly applied to intensive physical tasks such as manual welding and surface grinding12. These fabrication tasks involve sustained thermal stress, intermittent loud noise, awkward postures, and higher muscular energy expenditure, which the ILO recognizes as requiring extended recovery times11.

## **Work Center 1: Metal Cutting and Raw Material Processing**

The primary raw material for high-end outdoor furniture frames consists of architectural aluminum extrusions. While steel provides higher tensile strength, aluminum's low density, high thermal conductivity, and natural corrosion resistance make it the optimal choice for outdoor environments14. Industrial engineers must first dictate the specific alloy to be processed, as metallurgical properties directly dictate machining feed rates and tooling wear.

### **Metallurgical Selection: 6061-T6 versus 6063-T5**

The 6000-series aluminum alloys share magnesium and silicon as their primary alloying elements, but the subtle differences between 6061 and 6063 dramatically affect fabrication16. The 6061-T6 alloy is structurally superior, offering an ultimate tensile strength of 290 to 310 MPa and a yield strength of 240 to 276 MPa, which is roughly 30 to 40 percent stronger than 606315. However, 6061 achieves this high strength through the addition of copper and chromium15. This copper content introduces severe challenges in aesthetic surface finishing; when subjected to anodizing or certain chemical pre-treatments, 6061 can exhibit a dull, greyish, or inconsistent finish15. Furthermore, the copper content makes 6061 more susceptible to hot cracking during the welding process unless highly specific filler metals are utilized17.

Conversely, the 6063-T5 alloy features exceptional extrudability, a superior surface finish, and excellent aesthetic anodizing capabilities due to its purer composition17. While its yield strength is lower (160 to 214 MPa), its elongation at break is higher, making it significantly less prone to cracking during cold bending and forming operations15. Because premium outdoor furniture relies heavily on flawless aesthetic finishes and complex extruded profiles, 6063-T5 is the industry standard17. For the production of the standard club chair frame in this routing analysis, the base material is 16-gauge (0.065-inch wall thickness) 6063-T5 square tubing, specifically 2x2, 2x1, and 1.5x0.75-inch profiles.

### **Machining Parameters and Time Study**

Cutting aluminum extrusions efficiently without damaging the material or the tooling requires managing the surface feet per minute (SFPM). SFPM measures how fast the cutting edge of the blade moves against the material, functioning as a product of the machine's rotations per minute (RPM) and the blade diameter20. Operating outside the optimal SFPM range introduces catastrophic tooling failures. If the SFPM is too high, the blade teeth stop cutting and begin rubbing, generating immense friction that leads to tooth glazing—a phenomenon where a shiny, hardened layer forms on the tooth tips, destroying the cutting edge20. If the SFPM is too low, the blade will grab, deflect, or chip, putting severe stress on the machine spindle and the material20.

For non-ferrous aluminum profiles, the optimal cutting speed on an industrial cold saw ranges from 225 to 350 SFPM20. The higher end of this range is reserved for thin-walled tubing, such as the 16-gauge material used in this analysis, while the lower end is reserved for solid aluminum billets20.

To process a standard 2x2 16-gauge aluminum tube, the automated cold saw feed rate must be precisely calibrated. Industrial manufacturing data indicates that an automated or semi-automated cold saw processing thin-walled aluminum will complete the physical plunge cut in approximately 10 to 15 seconds, or 0.16 to 0.25 minutes21. However, an accurate industrial engineering time study must account for material handling, stock advancement, clamping, and part ejection.

* **Setup and Handling Time:** Utilizing a standard material follower and pneumatic bed clamps, stock advancement and registration take approximately 0.50 minutes per cut21.  
* **Active Cutting Time:** The physical plunge of the saw requires 0.25 minutes21.  
* **Normal Time Per Cut:** Combining setup and cutting yields a Normal Time of 0.75 minutes per individual cut.  
* **Standard Time Per Cut:** Applying the general 15 percent PF\&D allowance multiplier (1.15) results in an industry-standard time of **0.86 minutes per cut**.

A standard 34-inch by 34-inch outdoor club chair frame comprises 8 primary structural cuts (four vertical legs and four horizontal seat rails).

* **Total Normal Time:** 8 cuts multiplied by 0.75 minutes equals 6.0 minutes.  
* **Total Standard Time:** Applying the 15 percent PF\&D allowance yields a total Work Center Standard Time of **6.9 minutes per frame**.

## **Work Center 2: Welding and SMED Fixturing**

The welding work center universally represents the most critical constraint and primary bottleneck in aluminum furniture fabrication. Aluminum possesses excellent thermal conductivity, which dissipates heat rapidly, but it also features a low melting point14. Consequently, establishing a weld puddle requires significant, localized heat input to overcome the thermal dissipation, yet this heat must be tightly controlled to prevent a runaway puddle or complete burn-through of the thin 16-gauge material22. Furthermore, aluminum exhibits a high solidification shrinkage rate of approximately 6 percent23. This rapid thermal contraction introduces severe thermal distortion and warping during assembly, tearing the frame out of square if not properly restrained23.

### **GTAW versus GMAW Processing**

While Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW, or MIG) offers high deposition rates, continuous wire feeding, and travel speeds that yield high operating factors of 30 to 40 percent25, it generally lacks the aesthetic finesse required for luxury consumer goods. High-end outdoor furniture typically mandates the precision of Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW, or TIG). TIG allows for meticulous heat control and produces the coveted "stacked-dimes" aesthetic appearance by manually adding filler rod to cool the backside of the weld puddle rhythmically22.

The selection of filler wire is paramount when joining 6063-T5 aluminum. While ER5356 (containing 5 percent magnesium) offers higher shear strength, ER4043 (containing 5 percent silicon) is vastly superior for this application26. The ER4043 filler flows more smoothly, is highly crack-resistant, and crucially, prevents the weld seam from turning black if the frame is subjected to subsequent anodizing or aggressive chemical pre-treatments, ensuring a pristine finish under the powder coat26.

Modern inverter-based TIG power sources allow for precise manipulation of the alternating current (AC). Older equipment relied on a balanced 50-50 ratio of Electrode Negative (EN) to Electrode Positive (EP). Today, modern welding of thin aluminum requires a balance control set heavily toward EN (e.g., 75 percent EN to 25 percent EP) to maximize penetration while still providing enough EP cleaning action to strip the rapidly forming aluminum oxide layer22. An AC output frequency tuned between 150 and 250 Hz forces a tight, highly directional arc column, preventing the heat from spreading too far across the 16-gauge tubing and causing thermal distortion22. The general rule of thumb for aluminum amperage is one amp for every one-thousandth of an inch of material thickness; therefore, a 0.065-inch wall thickness requires approximately 65 amps as a baseline, though complex T-joints where heat dissipates in three directions may demand slightly more22.

### **Single Minute Exchange of Die (SMED) in Welding Fixtures**

Fixture setup historically consumes massive amounts of un-billable labor in fabrication shops. By implementing the Single Minute Exchange of Die (SMED) methodology, developed by Shigeo Shingo, setup times can be drastically reduced28. SMED focuses on converting "internal" setup time—tasks that must be done while the welding process is stopped—to "external" setup time—tasks that can be staged while the welder is actively working on a previous part28. The goal is to reduce changeovers and setup to single-digit minutes28.

For this welding work center, a customized modular fixture utilizing quick-release toggle clamps and integrated aluminum or copper heat sinks is deployed24. The heat sinks rapidly pull thermal energy away from the thin-walled 16-gauge tubing, mitigating the 6 percent solidification shrinkage and allowing for faster skip-welding sequences where the operator alternates weld locations to balance thermal input23. By pre-staging the cut tubing externally and utilizing one-touch pneumatic or manual toggle clamps instead of threaded bolts, the fixture setup time (Normal Time) is reduced to a highly efficient **3.0 minutes** per frame29.

![][image2]

### **TIG Welding Time-Study Calculations**

The calculation of welding time requires separating pure "arc time" from "clock time," which represents the total job time25.

* **Arc Speed (Time per Linear Inch):** For manual TIG welding of aluminum, standard travel speed is approximately 7.0 to 7.5 inches per minute (ipm)32. This equates to an active arc time of **0.13 to 0.14 minutes per linear inch**.  
* **Operating Factor:** TIG welding is a highly manual and ergonomically taxing process. The welder must feed filler rod by hand, continuously adjust the torch angle, reposition their body, and frequently pause to clean the rapidly forming oxide layer. These physical requirements restrict the arc to running only 20 to 25 percent of any given working hour25.

A standard 34-inch by 34-inch club chair frame involves approximately 12 primary joints. Assuming the use of 1.5-inch by 1.5-inch square tubing, each joint requires a 6-inch perimeter weld.

* **Total Linear Inches:** 12 joints multiplied by 6 inches equals 72 linear inches.  
* **Arc Time:** 72 linear inches divided by 7.5 ipm yields 9.6 minutes of pure, uninterrupted arc time.  
* **Total Clock Time (Normal Time):** Applying a conservative 22 percent operating factor25, the actual time the welder spends processing the frame on the table is 9.6 minutes divided by 0.22, equating to 43.6 minutes.  
* **Fixture Loading/Unloading:** 3.0 minutes via SMED principles.  
* **Total Base Time:** 43.6 minutes plus 3.0 minutes yields 46.6 minutes.

Because manual TIG welding involves heavy protective equipment, radiant heat exposure, and awkward sustained postures, the standard 15 percent allowance is insufficient. Consulting the ILO allowance parameters, a specialized 20 percent PF\&D allowance multiplier (1.20) is applied11. The **Industry Standard Time** for the complete TIG welding and fixturing of a single frame is calculated at **55.9 minutes**.

## **Work Center 3: Grinding and Surface Preparation**

Following the GTAW process, the aluminum frames must be mechanically finished. This involves removing any sharp edges, blending visible aesthetic welds flush with the parent material, and physically preparing the surface to guarantee the adhesion of the subsequent powder coating.

Aluminum's relatively low Brinell hardness (73 HB for 6063-T5) means the metal is highly ductile and prone to clogging standard abrasives15. Therefore, specialized aluminum-oxide or zirconia flap discs must be used to prevent material loading. In premium outdoor furniture, weld blending is a meticulous process; operators must grind the weld bead completely flat without undercutting or gouging the thin 0.065-inch parent metal.

Time studies indicate that grinding the top and outer visual faces of the 12 primary joints flush requires approximately 1.25 minutes of continuous abrasive action per joint.

* **Active Grinding Time:** 12 joints multiplied by 1.25 minutes equals 15.0 minutes of normal active labor per frame.  
* **Handling and Visual Inspection:** 2.0 minutes to rotate the frame and verify surface uniformity.  
* **Total Base Time:** 17.0 minutes.

Heavy mechanical grinding generates severe hand-arm vibration, high acoustic decibel levels, and requires significant muscular force to control the abrasive tool. Consulting the ILO allowance tables, tasks categorized as heavy work with intermittent loud noise and continuous standing warrant a maximum 20 percent PF\&D allowance to account for the physical toll and necessary acoustic and respiratory recovery4. Applying the 1.20 multiplier, the **Industry Standard Time** for the grinding work center is **20.4 minutes**.

## **Work Center 4: Powder Coating**

The powder coating process provides the primary aesthetic finish and the critical defense mechanism against UV degradation and environmental corrosion. This work center is unique because it combines active manual labor with passive, machine-controlled curing times. The complete process encompasses chemical pre-treatment, electrostatic powder application, and thermal curing33.

Time studies in powder coating must strictly isolate active labor from passive oven time. Active labor generates direct labor costs and dictates human resource allocation, while passive oven time dictates the overarching system throughput but does not require manual intervention. Failing to separate these times leads to grossly inaccurate labor routings.

### **Operational Sequence and Time Breakdown**

> 1. **Chemical Preparation and Hanging (Active Labor):** Before coating, the aluminum must undergo a conversion coating to improve adhesion and provide a secondary layer of corrosion protection33. Operators manually inspect the frame, wipe it down with a solvent to remove grinding dust, insert high-temperature silicone plugs into any threaded inserts, and hang the frame securely on the conveyor line. The Normal Time for these combined tasks is 5.0 minutes.  
> 2. **Electrostatic Spraying (Active Labor):** Utilizing a corona or tribo spray gun, the operator applies the thermoset polymer powder. A standard geometric club chair frame creates a high "Faraday cage" effect in the interior corners, where the electromagnetic field repels the charged powder. This phenomenon requires careful manual touch-ups and specific gun angle adjustments to ensure adequate coverage. The Normal Time for complete, even spraying is 4.0 minutes.  
> 3. **Thermal Curing (Passive Machine Time):** The coated frame enters a curing oven preheated to 400°F (204°C). The cross-linking of the polymer matrix requires the aluminum substrate to reach the target temperature, followed by a sustained dwell time to allow the powder to melt, flow, and cure into a continuous film. The Passive Time required for a standard extrusion is 20.0 minutes34.  
> 4. **Unhanging and Quality Control (Active Labor):** Once the frame has cooled sufficiently, it is removed from the conveyor, inspected for millage (thickness) consistency, and checked for defects such as orange peel or pinholing before being staged for final assembly. The Normal Time for unhanging and inspection is 3.0 minutes.

### **Standard Time Calculation**

The active manual labor required per frame totals 12.0 minutes (5.0 minutes prep \+ 4.0 minutes spray \+ 3.0 minutes unhang). Operating in a warm environment near the curing ovens with moderate physical exertion warrants the standard 15 percent PF\&D allowance10.

* **Active Labor Standard Time:** 12.0 minutes multiplied by 1.15 yields **13.8 minutes**.  
* **Total System Throughput Time:** 13.8 minutes of active labor plus 20.0 minutes of passive curing yields a total throughput time of 33.8 minutes.

For the purposes of the labor routing database, the recorded Industry Standard Time is exactly 13.8 minutes, as the 20-minute baking period requires zero human capital.

## **Work Center 5: Upholstery and Sewing**

Soft goods manufacturing in the premium outdoor furniture sector requires processing highly durable materials, specifically high-performance acrylic fabrics (such as Sunbrella) and high-density, reticulated open-cell polyurethane foam designed specifically to shed water and resist mold35.

The fabrication of a standard 24-inch by 24-inch outdoor box cushion involves precision pattern cutting, industrial sewing (including the integration of decorative piping and a hidden continuous coil zipper), and the physical compression and stuffing of the foam core. While thermal laser cutting is highly efficient for many textiles, automated oscillating CNC knives are strictly preferred in modern facilities processing treated outdoor fabrics. CNC knives eliminate the charred, heat-affected zones and the potentially toxic fumes associated with thermal laser cutting on chemically treated synthetic materials36.

### **MOST Analysis of Cushion Fabrication**

Breaking down the upholstery process via Standard Allowed Minutes (SAM) yields a highly predictable sequence of operations. The following Normal Times are established for the 24-inch box cushion:

> 1. **CNC Knife Cutting:** The automated cutting of the top and bottom fabric plates, the boxing strips (the vertical sides of the cushion), and the bias strips for the piping on a vacuum-assisted cutting table. Machine run time and manual unloading require 2.5 minutes38.  
> 2. **Sewing (Piping and Welting):** The operator folds the bias strip over the welt cord, sews it closed, and then attaches the completed welting to the perimeter of both the top and bottom fabric plates. The continuous nature of this sewing yields a Normal Time of 4.5 minutes.  
> 3. **Zipper Installation:** The operator inserts a continuous coil zipper into the rear boxing strip, sewing down both sides to secure it39. The Normal Time is 2.5 minutes.  
> 4. **Final Assembly Sewing:** The operator joins the four boxed corners of the side strips, then attaches the complete boxing strip to the top and bottom plates, ensuring perfect pattern matching and corner alignment39. The Normal Time is 5.0 minutes.  
> 5. **Foam Stuffing:** Using a vacuum foam compressor or a silk-film technique, the reticulated foam (pre-wrapped in a Dacron batting to crown the cushion) is mechanically compressed, inserted into the fabric casing, and zipped closed39. The Normal Time for this physical insertion is 3.5 minutes.

The total Base Time for the upholstery sequence is 18.0 minutes. Industrial sewing requires sustained, fine visual focus, which the ILO categorizes as a "fine or exacting" task requiring a 2 percent visual strain allowance12. Combined with a seated, somewhat constrained posture, the standard 15 percent PF\&D allowance is applied10. Applying the 1.15 multiplier to the 18.0-minute base time yields an **Industry Standard Time of 20.7 minutes** for the completion of one high-end box cushion.

## **Work Center 6: Stone Fabrication (Dekton)**

Premium outdoor dining tables increasingly feature ultra-compact sintered stone, such as Dekton, due to its absolute imperviousness to UV rays, extreme thermal shock, and scratching41. The creation of sintered stone involves milling raw minerals, atomizing them into a fine powder, and subjecting them to extreme pressure and a thermal process that mimics thousands of years of metamorphic rock formation in a matter of hours43. The resulting material is incredibly dense but highly brittle. It requires specific fabrication techniques, specialized continuous-rim diamond tooling, and precisely controlled slow CNC feed rates to prevent micro-fracturing and catastrophic structural failure during machining42.

### **Ergonomic Handling and OSHA Guidelines**

Sintered stone slabs are exceptionally heavy. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) does not provide a single numeric weight limit for manual lifting; rather, it enforces safe lifting protocols under the General Duty Clause, relying heavily on the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) equation45. Under ideal lifting conditions, NIOSH sets a threshold of 35 to 51 pounds for safe manual lifting45.

A full-size 72-inch by 36-inch (approximately 2cm thick) Dekton slab weighs hundreds of pounds, far exceeding this physiological limit. Consequently, industrial vacuum lifters and overhead gantry cranes are legally and operationally mandatory to move the material from the storage A-frame to the CNC bridge saw bed41. The careful rigging, lifting, and precise placement of the slab using these mechanical aids requires a Normal Time of 10.0 minutes.

### **CNC Machining Parameters**

Because sintered stone holds immense internal tension from the manufacturing process, the slab must first be perimeter-trimmed (approximately 1.5cm from the edge) to relieve stress before the final dimensional cut can be made41. The cutting bed must be perfectly flat, often utilizing rubber saddles to prevent any flex, with copious water flow directed precisely at the cut zone to prevent thermal shock cracks44.

According to the manufacturer's technical specifications, straight cutting requires a maximum feed rate of 0.7 to 0.9 meters per minute (m/min) utilizing a high spindle speed (2400 to 2600 RPM for a 300mm blade)48. Achieving a high-quality polished edge requires an even slower feed rate of 0.6 m/min41.

A 72-inch by 36-inch tabletop has a total perimeter of 216 inches, which converts mathematically to 5.48 meters.

* **CNC Cutting Time (at 0.8 m/min):** 5.48 meters divided by 0.8 m/min equals 6.85 minutes.  
* **CNC Edge Polishing Time (at 0.6 m/min):** 5.48 meters divided by 0.6 m/min equals 9.14 minutes.  
* **Relief Cutting and Automatic Tool Changes:** 4.0 minutes.  
* **Total Machining Time:** 19.99 minutes (rounded to 20.0 minutes).

The total Base Time for the stone fabrication process is 30.0 minutes (10.0 minutes of handling and setup plus 20.0 minutes of active CNC machining). Applying the standard 15 percent PF\&D allowance multiplier yields an **Industry Standard Time of 34.5 minutes** for the completion of the Dekton tabletop.

## **Consolidated Standard Routing Database**

The culmination of the time studies, ILO allowance integrations, kinematic analyses, and material feed-rate parameters yields the definitive routing database for the facility. This structured data establishes the foundational metrics required to accurately cost products, balance the manufacturing line, allocate labor, and determine the factory's overarching Takt time.

&nbsp;

| Work Center | Operation Name | Industry Standard Time (Minutes) | Justification & Calculation Methodology |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Metal Cutting** | Cold Saw Fabrication | **6.9** (Total) / *0.86 per cut* | Based on optimal 225-350 SFPM for 6063-T5 aluminum20. Assumes 8 structural cuts per frame. Includes 0.25 min cut time \+ 0.50 min stock advance21, plus a standard 15% PF\&D allowance10. |
| **Welding** | TIG Welding & Fixturing | **55.9** (Total) / *0.16 per inch* | Arc travel speed of 7.5 ipm32 equals \~0.13 min arc time per inch. 72 linear inches yields 9.6 mins pure arc time. Applied 22% operating factor yields 43.6 mins clock time25. SMED fixturing takes 3.0 mins28. Adjusted with a 20% heavy physical fatigue allowance4. |
| **Grinding/Prep** | Mechanical Flush Grinding | **20.4** | Assumes 12 primary joints at 1.25 mins of continuous grinding per joint using specialized flap discs to remove aluminum without undercutting. Includes 2 mins handling and a 20% heavy vibration/noise PF\&D allowance11. |
| **Powder Coating** | Prep, Spray, and Cure | **13.8** *(Active Labor Only)* | Distinguishes human labor from machine time. 5 mins prep/hang \+ 4 mins manual touch-up/spray \+ 3 mins unhang/QC. Includes 15% PF\&D allowance10. *(Note: Excludes 20 mins of passive oven cure time)*. |
| **Upholstery** | Box Cushion Fabrication | **20.7** | MOST analysis derived: 2.5 mins CNC knife cut38, 4.5 mins piping, 2.5 mins zipper39, 5 mins final assembly, 3.5 mins foam stuffing/compression. Includes 15% allowance factoring fine visual strain10. |
| **Stone Fab.** | Dekton CNC Route & Polish | **34.5** | Based on 5.48 linear meters of perimeter. CNC feed rates: 0.8 m/min for straight cut (6.85 mins) and 0.6 m/min for edge polishing (9.14 mins)41. Includes 10 mins vacuum-assisted handling46 and 15% allowance. |

## **Conclusion and Strategic Implementation**

The integration of these highly precise Standard Allowed Minutes into the facility's ERP system allows for exact cost-accounting, transparent labor routing, and dynamic capacity planning. By moving away from subjective estimations and relying on metallurgical realities, machine feed rates, and ILO-mandated fatigue allowances, the facility guarantees a sustainable production pace.

To optimize overall throughput and achieve continuous lean flow, management must focus fiercely on the identified system bottleneck: the GTAW (TIG) Welding process. Because welding consumes 55.9 standard minutes per frame—more than double the time of any other active labor process—the factory's overall Takt time will be entirely dictated by this specific workstation. To prevent upstream Work In Progress (WIP) accumulation at the saws and downstream starvation at the powder coating line, the facility must either allocate significantly more labor resources to the welding department compared to cutting and sewing, or invest further in advanced robotic weld automation to synchronize cycle times across the value stream31.
